younger.one_minute: Americans are choosing people for Congress, the group that helps make their country's laws. These votes happen halfway through a president's four-year term, so they are called midterms. Election Day is 3 November, but many people can vote earlier. Our papers follow what voters are deciding and how voting works.

who.name: Voters
who.about: People who choose who will represent them.

who.name: Congress
who.about: Two groups, the House and Senate, that help make US laws.

who.name: The main parties
who.about: Democrats and Republicans put forward candidates with different ideas.

who.name: Election officials
who.about: People who organise voting and count ballots under their state’s rules.

questions.a: They happen in the middle of a president's four-year term. People choose members of Congress, rather than a president.

questions.q: Why do some people vote early?
questions.a: Some states let voters cast a ballot before Election Day, in person or by mail. The options and deadlines depend on where a person lives.

questions.q: Do lots of early votes tell us who will win?
questions.a: No. The number of ballots cast is different from the number of votes each candidate receives. Votes still have to be counted.

older.one_minute: The US midterm elections take place on 3 November 2026, halfway through the president's four-year term. Voters choose members of the House of Representatives and Senate, whose majorities shape lawmaking, spending and oversight. Our coverage follows voter concerns, early voting and election rules. Early turnout figures describe participation; they do not establish which party or candidate has won.

who.name: Voters
who.about: Eligible citizens choosing representatives under their state’s voting rules.

who.name: Congress
who.about: The House and Senate; their party majorities shape legislation, spending and oversight.

who.name: Democrats and Republicans
who.about: The two main parties competing for seats in Congress.

who.name: State and local election officials
who.about: Administer voting, count ballots and report results under state law.

questions.q: What changes if a party gains control of a chamber?
questions.a: The majority chooses leaders and committee chairs and influences which legislation advances. Control of Congress affects how easily a president can pursue a legislative agenda.

questions.q: What do early-voting records tell us?
questions.a: They describe how many people have cast ballots at a particular stage. They do not establish who is winning. Comparisons also depend on dates, state rules and voting methods.

questions.q: Why do election rules differ across states?
questions.a: States administer elections under state and federal law. Registration deadlines, early-voting periods and voting methods can differ. Official state or local election websites provide the rules for a particular voter.
